text: Real datasets often have many columns that say nearly the same thing. A person's height in centimetres and in inches are two columns carrying one fact, and a hundred survey questions about mood may really measure a handful of underlying traits. Principal component analysis finds a few new directions that capture most of what the data does, so that we can describe each example with far fewer numbers. You met the intuition earlier in the course; now we put it to work.

Step one is to centre the data, subtracting the mean of each column so the cloud of points sits around the origin. Then we look for the direction along which the cloud is most spread out. Picture a cloud shaped like a cigar: its long axis is the first principal component, the single direction that keeps the most variation. The second component is the longest remaining direction at right angles to the first, and so on.

To find those directions, we build the covariance matrix, X transpose X divided by n minus one, where X is the centred data. Its eigenvectors are the principal directions, and each eigenvalue is the variance of the data along its direction, which is exactly how much spread that direction keeps. In practice, libraries usually take the singular value decomposition of the centred data instead, which gives the same directions with better numerical accuracy.

To compress, keep the top k directions as the columns of a matrix W, and project each centred example onto them: Z equals X times W. Each example is now k numbers instead of many. We can also go back: multiply Z by W transpose and add the mean, and we get a reconstruction that lies flat in the kept directions. Whatever the data did along the dropped directions is lost, and the reconstruction error measures exactly that.

How many components should we keep? Divide each eigenvalue by their total, and you get the fraction of the variance each direction explains. Plotted in order, these fractions usually fall steeply and then flatten, so a common rule is to keep enough components for their running total to reach some target, perhaps ninety or ninety-five percent.

A few practical cautions. Variance depends on units, so a column measured in rupees will swamp one measured in years unless you standardise the columns first. Like any preprocessing, the mean, the scaling and the directions should be fitted on the training set only. And principal components are blends of the original columns, so they are often hard to name, and because the method is linear, it cannot unroll data that lies on a curved surface.

When people draw pictures of word embeddings, with king near queen and Paris near France, they usually project hundreds of dimensions down to two, very often with exactly this method, so remember that such plots show only the directions of largest spread, not the whole space. That closes classical machine learning. Next, we build the neuron, a weighted sum followed by a bend.
